claim: Odor attraction in walking Drosophila melanogaster is commonly used to relate neural function to behavior.
source: Odor attraction in walking Drosophila melanogaster is commonly used to relate neural function to behavior, but the algorithms underlying attraction are unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established context for the study.

claim: The algorithms underlying odor attraction in walking Drosophila melanogaster are unclear.
source: Odor attraction in walking Drosophila melanogaster is commonly used to relate neural function to behavior, but the algorithms underlying attraction are unclear.
evidence: This is stated as the knowledge gap motivating the study.

claim: Odor evokes an upwind run during odor (ON response) in walking Drosophila.
source: We show that odor evokes two behaviors: an upwind run during odor (ON response), and a local search at odor offset (OFF response).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Odor evokes a local search at odor offset (OFF response) in walking Drosophila.
source: We show that odor evokes two behaviors: an upwind run during odor (ON response), and a local search at odor offset (OFF response).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Wind orientation requires antennal mechanoreceptors in walking Drosophila.
source: Wind orientation requires antennal mechanoreceptors, but search is driven solely by odor.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with antenna-stabilized flies shown in Figure 2.

claim: Search behavior is driven solely by odor in walking Drosophila.
source: Wind orientation requires antennal mechanoreceptors, but search is driven solely by odor.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with antenna-stabilized flies shown in Figure 2.

claim: A navigation model based on odor intensity and history can recapitulate the behavior of flies in the experimental apparatus.
source: Based on these data, we develop a navigation model that recapitulates the behavior of flies in our apparatus, and generates realistic trajectories when run in a turbulent boundary layer plume.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The navigation model generates realistic trajectories when run in a turbulent boundary layer plume.
source: Based on these data, we develop a navigation model that recapitulates the behavior of flies in our apparatus, and generates realistic trajectories when run in a turbulent boundary layer plume.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster has emerged as a leading model for understanding how neural circuits generate behavior.
source: Because of the genetic tools available in this organism, Drosophila melanogaster has emerged as a leading model for understanding how neural circuits generate behavior.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Olfactory behaviors in walking flies are central to studies of sensory processing.
source: Olfactory behaviors in walking flies lie at the heart of many studies of sensory processing (Root et al., 2008; Su et al., 2012), learning and memory (Aso et al., 2014; Owald et al., 2015), and the neural basis of hunger (Root et al., 2011; Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Olfactory behaviors in walking flies are central to studies of learning and memory.
source: Olfactory behaviors in walking flies lie at the heart of many studies of sensory processing (Root et al., 2008; Su et al., 2012), learning and memory (Aso et al., 2014; Owald et al., 2015), and the neural basis of hunger (Root et al., 2011; Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Olfactory behaviors in walking flies are central to studies of the neural basis of hunger.
source: Olfactory behaviors in walking flies lie at the heart of many studies of sensory processing (Root et al., 2008; Su et al., 2012), learning and memory (Aso et al., 2014; Owald et al., 2015), and the neural basis of hunger (Root et al., 2011; Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The precise algorithms by which walking flies locate an odor source are not clear.
source: However, the precise algorithms by which walking flies locate an odor source are not clear.
evidence: This is stated as the knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Algorithms for olfactory navigation can be broadly divided into two classes depending on whether organisms search in laminar or turbulent environments.
source: Algorithms for olfactory navigation have been studied in a number of species, and can be broadly divided into two classes, depending on whether the organisms typically search in a laminar environment or in a turbulent environment.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about navigation algorithms.

claim: In laminar environments, odor concentration provides a smooth directional cue that can be used to locate the odor source.
source: In laminar environments, odor concentration provides a smooth directional cue that can be used to locate the odor source.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about laminar navigation.

claim: Laminar navigators include bacteria.
source: Laminar navigators include bacteria (Brown and Berg, 1974), nematodes (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999), and Drosophila larvae (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brown and Berg, 1974.

claim: Laminar navigators include nematodes.
source: Laminar navigators include bacteria (Brown and Berg, 1974), nematodes (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999), and Drosophila larvae (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999.

claim: Laminar navigators include Drosophila larvae.
source: Laminar navigators include bacteria (Brown and Berg, 1974), nematodes (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999), and Drosophila larvae (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gomez-Marin et al., 2011 and Gershow et al., 2012.

claim: A key computation in laminar navigators is detection of temporal changes in odor concentration, which drives changes in the probability of re-orientation behaviors.
source: In each of these organisms, a key computation is detection of temporal changes in odor concentration, which drives changes in the probability of re-orientation behaviors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about laminar navigation mechanisms.

claim: In turbulent environments, odors are transported by the instantaneous structure of air or water currents, forming plumes with complex spatial and temporal structure.
source: In turbulent environments, odors are transported by the instantaneous structure of air or water currents, forming plumes with complex spatial and temporal structure (Crimaldi and Koseff, 2001; Crimaldi et al., 2002; Webster and Weissburg, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on turbulent plume structure.

claim: Within a turbulent plume, odor fluctuates continuously, meaning that instantaneous concentration gradients do not provide simple information about the direction of the source.
source: Within a turbulent plume, odor fluctuates continuously, meaning that instantaneous concentration gradients do not provide simple information about the direction of the source .
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about turbulent plumes.

claim: Navigation in turbulent environments has been studied most extensively in moths.
source: Navigation in turbulent environments has been studied most extensively in moths (Kennedy and Marsh, 1974; David et al., 1983; Baker, 1990; Kuenen and Carde, 1994; Rutkowski et al., 2009) but has also been investigated in flying adult Drosophila (van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014) and marine plankton (Page et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to moth navigation studies.

claim: Navigation in turbulent environments has been investigated in flying adult Drosophila.
source: Navigation in turbulent environments has been studied most extensively in moths (Kennedy and Marsh, 1974; David et al., 1983; Baker, 1990; Kuenen and Carde, 1994; Rutkowski et al., 2009) but has also been investigated in flying adult Drosophila (van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014) and marine plankton (Page et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014.

claim: Navigation in turbulent environments has been investigated in marine plankton.
source: Navigation in turbulent environments has been studied most extensively in moths (Kennedy and Marsh, 1974; David et al., 1983; Baker, 1990; Kuenen and Carde, 1994; Rutkowski et al., 2009) but has also been investigated in flying adult Drosophila (van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014) and marine plankton (Page et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Page et al., 2011.

claim: In turbulent navigators, the onset or presence of odor drives upwind or upstream orientation.
source: In these organisms, the onset or presence of odor drives upwind or upstream orientation, while loss of odor drives casting orthogonal to the direction of flow.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about turbulent navigation behaviors.

claim: In turbulent navigators, loss of odor drives casting orthogonal to the direction of flow.
source: In these organisms, the onset or presence of odor drives upwind or upstream orientation, while loss of odor drives casting orthogonal to the direction of flow.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about turbulent navigation behaviors.

claim: Laminar navigation algorithms depend only on the dynamics of odor concentration.
source: An important distinction between laminar and turbulent navigation algorithms is that the former depend only on the dynamics of odor concentration, while the latter rely also on measurements of flow direction derived from mechanosensation or optic flow (Cardé and Willis, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as an established distinction between navigation types, supported by citation.

claim: Turbulent navigation algorithms rely on measurements of flow direction derived from mechanosensation or optic flow.
source: An important distinction between laminar and turbulent navigation algorithms is that the former depend only on the dynamics of odor concentration, while the latter rely also on measurements of flow direction derived from mechanosensation or optic flow (Cardé and Willis, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as an established distinction between navigation types, supported by citation.

claim: The role of temporal cues in turbulent navigation is unclear.
source: Also unclear is the role of temporal cues in turbulent navigation.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Several studies have suggested that precise timing information about plume fluctuations might be important for navigation.
source: Several studies have suggested that precise timing information about plume fluctuations might be important for navigation (Baker, 1990; Mafra-Neto and Cardé, 1994), or that algorithms keeping track of the detailed history of odor encounters may promote chemotaxis (Vergassola et al., 2007), but the relationship between odor dynamics and olfactory behaviors has been challenging to measure experimentally (Pang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baker, 1990 and Mafra-Neto and Cardé, 1994.

claim: Algorithms keeping track of the detailed history of odor encounters may promote chemotaxis.
source: Several studies have suggested that precise timing information about plume fluctuations might be important for navigation (Baker, 1990; Mafra-Neto and Cardé, 1994), or that algorithms keeping track of the detailed history of odor encounters may promote chemotaxis (Vergassola et al., 2007), but the relationship between odor dynamics and olfactory behaviors has been challenging to measure experimentally (Pang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vergassola et al., 2007.

claim: The relationship between odor dynamics and olfactory behaviors has been challenging to measure experimentally.
source: Several studies have suggested that precise timing information about plume fluctuations might be important for navigation (Baker, 1990; Mafra-Neto and Cardé, 1994), or that algorithms keeping track of the detailed history of odor encounters may promote chemotaxis (Vergassola et al., 2007), but the relationship between odor dynamics and olfactory behaviors has been challenging to measure experimentally (Pang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pang et al., 2018.

claim: Olfactory navigation in walking flies has not been studied as quantitatively as in other organisms.
source: In comparison to these studies, olfactory navigation in walking flies has not been studied as quantitatively.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap motivating the current study.

claim: A walking fly in nature will encounter an odor plume that is developing close to a solid boundary.
source: A walking fly in nature will encounter an odor plume that is developing close to a solid boundary.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the natural environment for walking flies.

claim: Boundary layer plumes are broader than airborne plumes.
source: Such plumes are broader, exhibit slower fluctuations, and allow odor to persist further downwind from the source, compared to the airborne plumes encountered by flying organisms (Crimaldi and Koseff, 2001; Crimaldi et al., 2002; Webster and Weissburg, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on plume characteristics.

claim: Boundary layer plumes exhibit slower fluctuations than airborne plumes.
source: Such plumes are broader, exhibit slower fluctuations, and allow odor to persist further downwind from the source, compared to the airborne plumes encountered by flying organisms (Crimaldi and Koseff, 2001; Crimaldi et al., 2002; Webster and Weissburg, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on plume characteristics.

claim: Boundary layer plumes allow odor to persist further downwind from the source compared to airborne plumes.
source: Such plumes are broader, exhibit slower fluctuations, and allow odor to persist further downwind from the source, compared to the airborne plumes encountered by flying organisms (Crimaldi and Koseff, 2001; Crimaldi et al., 2002; Webster and Weissburg, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on plume characteristics.

claim: Navigational strategies in boundary layer and airborne environments might be different.
source: Navigational strategies in these two environments might therefore be different.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences in plume characteristics between the two environments.

claim: Walking flies have been shown to turn upwind when encountering an attractive odor.
source: In laboratory studies, walking flies have been shown to turn upwind when encountering an attractive odor (Flügge, 1934; Steck et al., 2012), and downwind when odor is lost (Bell and Wilson, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Flügge, 1934 and Steck et al., 2012.

claim: Walking flies have been shown to turn downwind when odor is lost.
source: In laboratory studies, walking flies have been shown to turn upwind when encountering an attractive odor (Flügge, 1934; Steck et al., 2012), and downwind when odor is lost (Bell and Wilson, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bell and Wilson, 2016.

claim: Flies can stay within an odorized region when wind cues provide no direction information by modulating multiple parameters of their locomotion.
source: However, flies can also stay within an odorized region when wind cues provide no direction information, by modulating multiple parameters of their locomotion (Jung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jung et al., 2015.

claim: Walking flies have been shown to turn towards the antenna that receives a higher odor concentration.
source: Finally, walking flies have been shown to turn towards the antenna that receives a higher odor concentration (Borst and Heisenberg, 1982; Gaudry et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borst and Heisenberg, 1982 and Gaudry et al., 2013.

claim: It is not clear how diverse motor programs work together to promote navigation toward an attractive odor source in complex natural environments.
source: It is not clear how these diverse motor programs work together to promote navigation toward an attractive odor source in complex natural environments.
evidence: This is stated as the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The miniature wind-tunnel paradigm allows precise control of wind and odor stimuli delivered to freely walking flies.
source: To investigate the specific responses underlying olfactory navigation, we developed a miniature wind-tunnel apparatus in which we could present well-controlled wind and odor stimuli to walking flies (Figure 1A and B and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is described as a methodological development and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Flies were exposed to a constant flow of filtered, humidified air at 11.9 cm/s in the behavioral arena.
source: Flies were placed in rectangular arenas, where they were exposed to a constant flow of filtered, humidified air, defining the wind direction. Into this airflow we injected pulses of odor with rapid onset and offset kinetics, producing a front of odor that was transported down the arena at 11.9 cm/s.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail and confirmed by measurements in Figure 1E.

claim: Odor pulses had rapid onset and offset kinetics in the behavioral apparatus.
source: Into this airflow we injected pulses of odor with rapid onset and offset kinetics, producing a front of odor that was transported down the arena at 11.9 cm/s.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Genetically blind flies (norpA36 mutants) were used to remove any possible contribution of visual responses.
source: We used genetically blind flies (norpA36 mutants) in order to remove any possible contribution of visual responses.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice to isolate olfactory responses.

claim: Flies were starved 5 hr prior to the experiment.
source: Flies were starved 5 hr prior to the experiment, and were tested for approximately 2 hr (from ZT 2–4), in a series of 70 second-long trials with blank (wind only) and odor trials randomly interleaved.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail.

claim: Flies were tested for approximately 2 hr from ZT 2-4.
source: Flies were starved 5 hr prior to the experiment, and were tested for approximately 2 hr (from ZT 2–4), in a series of 70 second-long trials with blank (wind only) and odor trials randomly interleaved.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail.

claim: In the presence of 10% apple cider vinegar, flies oriented upwind and moved faster and straighter.
source: We observed that in the presence of 10% apple cider vinegar (ACV), flies oriented upwind, and moved faster and straighter (Figure 1C, magenta traces).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C and quantified in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Following odor offset, flies exhibited more tortuous and localized trajectories.
source: Following odor offset, flies exhibited more tortuous and localized trajectories (Figure 1C, cyan traces).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The OFF response resembles local search behavior observed in other insects.
source: This 'OFF' response resembles local search behavior observed in other insects (Willis et al., 2008), and persisted for tens of seconds after odor offset.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Willis et al., 2008 and data in Figure 1F.

claim: The OFF response persisted for tens of seconds after odor offset.
source: This 'OFF' response resembles local search behavior observed in other insects (Willis et al., 2008), and persisted for tens of seconds after odor offset.
evidence: This is observed in the behavioral data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: On trials without odor, flies tended to aggregate at the downwind end of the arena.
source: On trials without odor, flies tended to aggregate at the downwind end of the arena (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: During odor presentation, upwind velocity and ground speed both increased significantly.
source: During odor presentation, upwind velocity (i.e. speed of flies along the longitudinal axis of the arenas) and ground speed both increased significantly, while angular velocity and curvature (i.e. ratio between angular velocity and ground speed) decreased after an initial peak.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1F-G with statistical tests.

claim: During odor presentation, angular velocity and curvature decreased after an initial peak.
source: During odor presentation, upwind velocity (i.e. speed of flies along the longitudinal axis of the arenas) and ground speed both increased significantly, while angular velocity and curvature (i.e. ratio between angular velocity and ground speed) decreased after an initial peak.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1F-G.

claim: The initial peak observed in angular velocity and curvature corresponds to big turns performed by flies to orient upwind after odor onset.
source: This resulted in the straighter trajectories observed during odor; the initial peak observed in angular velocity and curvature corresponds to big turns performed by flies to orient upwind after odor onset.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Following odor offset, angular velocity increased.
source: Following odor offset, angular velocity increased, while ground speed decreased, resulting in the increased curvature characteristic of local search (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1F-G with statistical tests.

claim: Following odor offset, ground speed decreased.
source: Following odor offset, angular velocity increased, while ground speed decreased, resulting in the increased curvature characteristic of local search (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1F-G with statistical tests.

claim: Turn probability increased after odor offset.
source: Since an increase in probability of reorientation has been traditionally identified as a hallmark of localized search (Brown and Berg, 1974; Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999; Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012), we calculated the turn probability of flies in our arena as a binarized version of curvature around a threshold of 20 deg/mm. Indeed, turn probability increased as well after odor offset (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1F-G with statistical tests.

claim: Upwind velocity became negative after odor offset.
source: Upwind velocity also became negative after odor offset, although this response was weaker than the upwind orientation during odor, and peaked later than the changes in ground speed and curvature.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1F.

claim: The negative upwind velocity response after odor offset was weaker than the upwind orientation during odor.
source: Upwind velocity also became negative after odor offset, although this response was weaker than the upwind orientation during odor, and peaked later than the changes in ground speed and curvature.
evidence: This is observed by comparing responses in Figure 1F.

claim: The negative upwind velocity response peaked later than the changes in ground speed and curvature.
source: Upwind velocity also became negative after odor offset, although this response was weaker than the upwind orientation during odor, and peaked later than the changes in ground speed and curvature.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1F.

claim: There was considerable variability between individuals in ON and OFF responses.
source: Although most of the flies we tested showed ON and OFF responses as described above, we observed considerable variability between individuals (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Motor parameters from the same individual in different trials were correlated.
source: Motor parameters from the same individual in different trials were correlated, whereas parameters randomly selected from different individuals were not (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Motor parameters randomly selected from different individuals were not correlated.
source: Motor parameters from the same individual in different trials were correlated, whereas parameters randomly selected from different individuals were not (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: There was a slight tendency for responses to be weaker during the first few trials.
source: There was a slight tendency for responses to be weaker during the first few trials; afterwards, this behavior was stable (on average) across the entire experimental session (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: After the first few trials, behavior was stable on average across the entire experimental session.
source: There was a slight tendency for responses to be weaker during the first few trials; afterwards, this behavior was stable (on average) across the entire experimental session (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Sighted flies of the same genetic background showed ON and OFF responses.
source: Sighted flies of the same genetic background also showed ON and OFF responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), with increases in upwind velocity and ground speed during odor, and increases in angular velocity and decreased ground speed after odor offset.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The increase in angular velocity appeared to be weaker in sighted flies compared to blind flies.
source: However, the increase in angular velocity appeared to be weaker, on average, in these flies.
evidence: This is observed by comparing data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 to Figure 1.

claim: Apple cider vinegar drives an ON response consisting of upwind orientation coupled with faster and straighter trajectories.
source: Together, these data indicate that apple cider vinegar drives two distinct behavioral responses: an ON response consisting of upwind orientation coupled with faster and straighter trajectories, and an OFF response consisting of slower and more curved trajectories.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figure 1.

claim: Apple cider vinegar drives an OFF response consisting of slower and more curved trajectories.
source: Together, these data indicate that apple cider vinegar drives two distinct behavioral responses: an ON response consisting of upwind orientation coupled with faster and straighter trajectories, and an OFF response consisting of slower and more curved trajectories.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figure 1.

claim: Optogenetic activation of orco+ neurons did not elicit attraction unless wind was present.
source: Previous studies have found that optogenetic activation of orco+ neurons did not elicit attraction (Suh et al., 2007), unless wind was present (Bell and Wilson, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Suh et al., 2007 and Bell and Wilson, 2016.

claim: Modulation of gait parameters by odor has been observed when the wind is directed perpendicular to the plane of the arena.
source: However, modulation of gait parameters by odor has also been observed when the wind is directed perpendicular to the plane of the arena (Jung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jung et al., 2015.

claim: Stabilizing the third segment of the antennae using UV glue renders flies 'wind-blind'.
source: To ask whether walking flies could respond to odor in the absence of wind, we stabilized the third segment of the antennae using a small drop of UV glue. Fruit flies sense wind direction using stretch receptors that detect rotations of the third antennal segment (Yorozu et al., 2009). This manipulation therefore renders flies 'wind-blind' (Budick et al., 2007; Bhandawat et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach supported by citations.

claim: Fruit flies sense wind direction using stretch receptors that detect rotations of the third antennal segment.
source: Fruit flies sense wind direction using stretch receptors that detect rotations of the third antennal segment (Yorozu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yorozu et al., 2009.

claim: Wind-blind flies showed severely impaired directional responses to odor and wind.
source: We found that wind-blind flies showed severely impaired directional responses to odor and wind.
evidence: This is a primary finding shown in Figure 2.

claim: Upwind velocity was not significantly modulated in wind-blind flies either during or after odor.
source: Upwind velocity was not significantly modulated either during the odor or after (Figure 2A–B, top).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A-B with statistical tests.

claim: The downwind positional bias seen in the absence of odor was reduced in wind-blind flies.
source: In addition, the downwind positional bias seen in the absence of odor was reduced (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The average arena position of wind-blind flies on no-odor trials was no different from that of intact flies in the absence of wind.
source: The average arena position of wind-blind flies on no-odor trials was no different from that of intact flies in the absence of wind (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with statistical tests.

claim: Antennal wind sensors are critical for the oriented components of olfactory search behavior.
source: Thus, antennal wind sensors are critical for the oriented components of olfactory search behavior.
evidence: This is concluded from the wind-blind fly experiments in Figure 2.

claim: Wind-blind flies still responded to odor by modulating their ground speed and angular velocity.
source: However, wind-blind flies still responded to odor by modulating their ground speed and angular velocity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Wind-blind flies increased their curvature after odor offset.
source: Wind-blind flies increased their curvature after odor offset and also increased their ground speed during odor (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B with statistical tests.

claim: Wind-blind flies increased their ground speed during odor.
source: Wind-blind flies increased their curvature after odor offset and also increased their ground speed during odor (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B with statistical tests.

claim: Odor can directly modulate gait parameters to influence navigation in the absence of wind.
source: These results imply that odor can directly modulate gait parameters to influence navigation in the absence of wind.
evidence: This is concluded from the wind-blind fly experiments in Figure 2.

claim: Olfactory navigation depends on multimodal processing (odor-gated upwind orientation).
source: Together these experiments show that olfactory navigation depends both on multimodal processing (odor-gated upwind orientation), and on direct transformation of odor signals into changes in ground speed and curvature.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Olfactory navigation depends on direct transformation of odor signals into changes in ground speed and curvature.
source: Together these experiments show that olfactory navigation depends both on multimodal processing (odor-gated upwind orientation), and on direct transformation of odor signals into changes in ground speed and curvature.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Both upwind velocity during odor and turn probability after offset grew with increasing odor concentration between 0.01% and 1%.
source: We found that both upwind velocity during odor and turn probability after offset grew with increasing odor concentration between 0.01% and 1%, but saturated or even decreased at 10% (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Both upwind velocity during odor and turn probability after offset saturated or decreased at 10% odor concentration.
source: We found that both upwind velocity during odor and turn probability after offset grew with increasing odor concentration between 0.01% and 1%, but saturated or even decreased at 10% (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The fitted Hill coefficient was very close to 1 (1.03 for ON and 1.06 for OFF).
source: The fitted Hill coefficient was very close to 1 (1.03 for ON and 1.06 for OFF).
evidence: This is a result from fitting the data in Figure 3A-B.

claim: A saturating Hill function nonlinearity is expected from odor transduction kinetics.
source: A saturating Hill function nonlinearity is to be expected from odor transduction kinetics, and has been found to describe encoding of odor stimuli by peripheral olfactory receptor neurons (Kaissling et al., 1987; Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Schulze et al., 2015), and central olfactory projection neurons (Olsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on odor transduction.

claim: A decrease in response at the highest odor intensities could arise from inhibitory glomeruli that are recruited at higher odor intensity.
source: A decrease in response at the highest intensities could arise from inhibitory glomeruli that are recruited at higher odor intensity, as has been described in Semmelhack and Wang, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation.

claim: Turn probability began to grow gradually as soon as the odor concentration started to decrease during off-ramps.
source: We observed that turn probability began to grow gradually as soon as the odor concentration started to decrease (Figure 3D, white arrow), but peaked close to the point where the linear off ramp returned to baseline (black arrow).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Turn probability peaked close to the point where the linear off ramp returned to baseline.
source: We observed that turn probability began to grow gradually as soon as the odor concentration started to decrease (Figure 3D, white arrow), but peaked close to the point where the linear off ramp returned to baseline (black arrow).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The off-ramp results suggest some form of sensitivity adaptation that allows the fly to respond to a small decrease from a saturating concentration of odor.
source: This result suggests some form of sensitivity adaptation, that allows the fly to respond to a small decrease from a saturating concentration of odor.
evidence: This is inferred from the off-ramp data in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Upwind velocity remained positive during odor off-ramps.
source: We also noted that upwind velocity remained positive during these ramps (Figure 3C, white arrow), suggesting that ON and OFF responses can be driven —at least partially— at the same time.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ON and OFF responses can be driven at least partially at the same time.
source: We also noted that upwind velocity remained positive during these ramps (Figure 3C, white arrow), suggesting that ON and OFF responses can be driven —at least partially— at the same time.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation in Figure 3C.

claim: Olfactory receptor neurons can follow odor fluctuations up to 10-20 Hz.
source: Indeed, olfactory receptor neurons can follow odor fluctuations up to 10–20 Hz (Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Kim et al., 2011), and these rapid responses have been hypothesized to be critical for navigation in odor plumes (Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nagel and Wilson, 2011 and Kim et al., 2011.

claim: Rapid olfactory receptor neuron responses have been hypothesized to be critical for navigation in odor plumes.
source: Indeed, olfactory receptor neurons can follow odor fluctuations up to 10–20 Hz (Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Kim et al., 2011), and these rapid responses have been hypothesized to be critical for navigation in odor plumes (Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nagel and Wilson, 2011 and Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017.

claim: The peak frequency that could be presented was limited to 1 Hz because higher frequencies became attenuated at the downwind end of the arena.
source: The peak frequency we could present was limited to 1 Hz, as we found that frequencies higher than this became attenuated at the downwind end of the arena, presumably because odor diffuses as it is transported downwind, blurring the differences between peaks and troughs in the stimulus (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological limitation.

claim: Upwind velocity tracked odor fluctuations at the lowest frequencies but modulation became attenuated at higher frequencies.
source: We found that upwind velocity tracked odor fluctuations at the lowest frequencies, but that modulation became attenuated at higher frequencies (end of the ascending frequency sweep and start of the descending frequency sweep; Figure 3E and G), suggesting low-pass filtering of the odor signal.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E and G.

claim: The attenuation of upwind velocity at higher frequencies suggests low-pass filtering of the odor signal.
source: We found that upwind velocity tracked odor fluctuations at the lowest frequencies, but that modulation became attenuated at higher frequencies (end of the ascending frequency sweep and start of the descending frequency sweep; Figure 3E and G), suggesting low-pass filtering of the odor signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 3E and G.

claim: Upwind velocity peaked in response to nearly every fluctuation in the 'plume walk' but remained elevated during clusters of odor fluctuations.
source: Similarly, upwind velocity peaked in response to nearly every fluctuation in the 'plume walk', but remained elevated during clusters of odor fluctuations (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The frequency-dependent attenuation was seen in both ascending and descending frequency sweeps, arguing against it being an effect of position in the arena or duration of exposure to odor.
source: The frequency-dependent attenuation was seen in both ascending and descending frequency sweeps, arguing against it being an effect of position in the arena, or duration of exposure to odor.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing data in Figure 3E and G.

claim: Attenuation was not due to the filter imposed on trajectories during processing.
source: Attenuation was not due to the filter imposed on trajectories during processing, as it was visible also when this filtering step was omitted (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Rapid decreases in ground speed in response to click stimuli did not attenuate at higher frequencies.
source: We observed rapid decreases in ground speed in response to click stimuli that did not attenuate at higher frequencies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,F), arguing that the attenuation seen with odor does not reflect a limit on detecting rapid behavioral responses.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,F.

claim: Turn probability at offset showed even stronger evidence of low-pass filtering than upwind velocity.
source: Turn probability at offset showed even stronger evidence of low-pass filtering.
evidence: This is observed by comparing Figure 3F,H,J to Figure 3E,G,I.

claim: Fluctuations in turn probability were attenuated during the higher frequencies of both frequency sweeps.
source: Fluctuations in turn probability were attenuated during the higher frequencies of both frequency sweeps, and the strongest responses occurred at the end of the stimulus to the absence of odor (Figure 3F,H,J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F,H,J.

claim: The strongest turn probability responses occurred at the end of the stimulus to the absence of odor.
source: Fluctuations in turn probability were attenuated during the higher frequencies of both frequency sweeps, and the strongest responses occurred at the end of the stimulus to the absence of odor (Figure 3F,H,J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F,H,J.

claim: ON and OFF responses depend on odor history in different ways, with rapid fluctuations leading to elevated ON responses and suppressed OFF responses.
source: Together these experiments provide detailed measurements of the way that ON and OFF behaviors depend on the history of odor encounters. Moreover, they suggest that the two responses depend on odor history in different ways, with rapid fluctuations leading to elevated ON responses and suppressed OFF responses.
evidence: This is concluded from the frequency sweep and plume walk experiments in Figure 3.

claim: Behavioral responses saturated at concentrations above 1% ACV and were also modulated by small decreases and fluctuations from a higher concentration (10%).
source: A challenge was that behavioral responses saturated at concentrations above 1% ACV, and they were also modulated by small decreases and fluctuations from a higher concentration (10%).
evidence: This is observed in the data from Figure 3.

claim: The behavioral data suggest some form of adaptation in which the sensitivity of behavior to odorant shifts over time.
source: This suggests some form of adaptation, in which the sensitivity of behavior to odorant shifts over time, allowing responses to occur near what was previously a saturating concentration.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data in Figure 3.

claim: Sensitivity adaptation has been described at the level of olfactory receptor neuron transduction.
source: Sensitivity adaptation has been described at the level of olfactory receptor neuron transduction and can be implemented as a slow rightward shift in the Hill function that describes intensity encoding (Kaissling et al., 1987; Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on ORN adaptation.

claim: The ACF model (adaptive compression followed by filtering) outperformed other ON models.
source: We found that both models with adaptation performed better than models without, and that the model with adaptive compression first ('ACF', Figure 4A) outperformed the adaptive model with filtering first ('FAC', Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The ACF ON model correctly predicted saturation with increasing odor concentration.
source: As shown in Figure 4C, model ACF correctly predicted saturation with increasing odor concentration, and also the fact that responses to high odor concentrations exhibit adaptation while those to low odor concentrations do not.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ACF ON model correctly predicted that responses to high odor concentrations exhibit adaptation while those to low odor concentrations do not.
source: As shown in Figure 4C, model ACF correctly predicted saturation with increasing odor concentration, and also the fact that responses to high odor concentrations exhibit adaptation while those to low odor concentrations do not.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ACF ON model correctly predicted the attenuation seen during frequency sweeps.
source: This model also correctly predicted the attenuation seen during frequency sweeps (Figure 4D and E), although some details of response timing early in the stimulus were not matched.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: The time constant of filtering for the ON model was 0.72 s, significantly slower than encoding in peripheral ORNs.
source: The time constant of filtering was 0.72 s (see Table 1), significantly slower than encoding in peripheral ORNs (Kim et al., 2011; Nagel and Wilson, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a result from model fitting, with comparison to cited ORN studies.

claim: The time constant of adaptation for the ON model was very slow (9.8 s).
source: The time constant of adaptation was very slow (9.8 s).
evidence: This is stated as a result from model fitting shown in Table 1.

claim: Models without adaptation exhibited strong saturation during the frequency sweep, which was not observed experimentally.
source: Models without adaptation (pink trace in Figure 4D–E) exhibited strong saturation during the frequency sweep, which was not observed experimentally.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: The ACF OFF model (adaptive compression followed by filtering) outperformed other OFF models.
source: Again we found that models with adaptation outperformed those without, and that the adaptive model with compression first very slightly outperformed the adaptive model with filtering first (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The ACF OFF model reproduced reasonably well the responses of flies to odor ramps.
source: This model reproduced reasonably well the responses of flies to odor ramps (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The slow time constant of filtering for the OFF model was 4.84 s, accounting for the selectivity of the OFF response to low frequencies during frequency sweeps.
source: The slow time constant of filtering was 4.84 s, accounting for the selectivity of the OFF response to low frequencies during frequency sweeps (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: This is stated as a result from model fitting shown in Table 1, with interpretation based on Figure 4I and J.

claim: The time constant of adaptation for the OFF model was of similar magnitude to that derived from fitting the ON response (10.62 s).
source: The time constant of adaptation was of similar magnitude to that derived from fitting the ON response (10.62 s).
evidence: This is stated as a result from model fitting shown in Table 1.

claim: The ON model reproduced most major contours in the 'plume walk' response.
source: We found that the ON model reproduced most major contours in the 'plume walk' response (Figure 4K), although there was some discrepancy in the timing of peaks early in the response as for the frequency sweeps (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The OFF model captured many of the major peaks in the behavioral response to the plume walk.
source: The OFF model also captured many of the major peaks in the behavioral response (Figure 4L), as well as the time course of the slow offset response after the end of the stimulus.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4L.

claim: The OFF model captured the time course of the slow offset response after the end of the plume walk stimulus.
source: The OFF model also captured many of the major peaks in the behavioral response (Figure 4L), as well as the time course of the slow offset response after the end of the stimulus.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4L.

claim: The RMSE errors between predictions and data for the plume walks were comparable to those for the stimuli used for fitting.
source: Overall, the RMSE errors between predictions and data for the plume walks were comparable to those for the stimuli we used for fitting.
evidence: This is stated as a result from model testing.

claim: Models featuring adaptive compression followed by linear filtering provide a good fit to behavioral dynamics over a wide range of stimuli.
source: We conclude that models featuring adaptive compression followed by linear filtering provide a good fit to behavioral dynamics over a wide range of stimuli.
evidence: This is concluded from the model fitting and testing results in Figure 4.

claim: In the navigation model, odor dynamics directly influence ground speed and turn probability through the ON and OFF functions.
source: In our model (Figure 5A–C), we propose that odor dynamics directly influence ground speed and turn probability through the ON and OFF functions developed and fit above.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the navigation model shown in Figure 5.

claim: The average angular velocity as a function of wind direction in the period immediately after odor onset had a strong 'upwind' shape.
source: Supporting the notion of a wind direction-based D-function, we found that the average angular velocity as a function of wind direction in the period immediately after odor onset had a strong 'upwind' shape (Figure 5D, magenta trace), while the angular velocity after odor offset had a weaker 'downwind' shape (Figure 5D, black trace).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The angular velocity after odor offset had a weaker 'downwind' shape.
source: Supporting the notion of a wind direction-based D-function, we found that the average angular velocity as a function of wind direction in the period immediately after odor onset had a strong 'upwind' shape (Figure 5D, magenta trace), while the angular velocity after odor offset had a weaker 'downwind' shape (Figure 5D, black trace).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The navigation model produced upwind runs during the odor pulse and searching after odor offset, similar to real flies.
source: Similar to real flies, this model produced upwind runs during the odor pulse and searching after odor offset (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Average upwind velocity during odor and turn probability after odor in the model were comparable to measurements from real flies.
source: Average upwind velocity during the odor and turn probability after the odor were comparable to measurements from real flies (compare Figure 5G and Figure 1G).
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figure 5G and Figure 1G.

claim: The wind-blind model produced undirected runs during odor and search behavior at odor offset, as in wind-blind real flies.
source: In this case, the model produced undirected runs during odor and search behavior at odor offset, as in our data (compare Figure 5H–I and Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figure 5H-I and Figure 2A-B.

claim: Scaling the ON and OFF functions to match individual flies produced trajectories that resembled the behavior of those flies both qualitatively and quantitatively.
source: The trajectories produced by these scaled models resembled the behavior of individual flies both qualitatively and quantitatively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5J-K.

claim: The navigation model captures essential features of how flies respond to odor and wind in miniature wind-tunnels.
source: Together, these results support the idea that our model captures essential features of how flies respond to odor and wind in miniature wind-tunnels, including the responses of intact and wind-blind flies, and variations in behavior across individuals.
evidence: This is concluded from the model simulations in Figure 5.

claim: Two equivalent wind tunnels were constructed, one in New York for behavioral experiments and one in Colorado for plume measurements.
source: To that end we constructed two equivalent wind tunnels capable of delivering a turbulent odor plume (Figure 6A; see Materials and methods). In one tunnel (New York), we incorporated IR lighting below the bed and cameras above it to image fly behavior in response to a turbulent odor plume. In the second tunnel (Colorado), we used a UV laser light sheet and acetone vapor to obtain to high-resolution movies of the plume for use in modeling (Figure 6B, Connor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach.

claim: The shape and dynamics of the plume in the New York tunnel was similar to the one measured in Colorado.
source: We used photo-ionization detector measurements to corroborate that the shape and dynamics of the plume in the New York tunnel was similar to the one measured in Colorado (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Flies uniformly preferred the downwind end of the arena with wind only (no odor).
source: We first tested flies with wind only (no odor) at 10 cm/s. As in our miniature wind tunnels, we found that flies uniformly preferred the downwind end of the arena (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the absence of wind, the downwind preference was reduced.
source: In the absence of wind, this preference was reduced (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Of 66 flies tested in the turbulent plume, 37 (56%) successfully located the odor source.
source: Of 66 flies, 37 (56%) successfully located the odor source, walking upwind and lingering in a small region close to the odor tube (Figure 6E, left trace).
evidence: This is stated as a result from behavioral experiments.

claim: 18% of flies searched in the middle of the arena without getting close to the source.
source: Other flies searched in the middle of the arena without getting close to the source (Figure 6E, middle trace, 18%), while others headed downwind and remained at the downwind end of the arena (Figure 6E, right trace, 15%).
evidence: This is stated as a result from behavioral experiments.

claim: 15% of flies headed downwind and remained at the downwind end of the arena.
source: Other flies searched in the middle of the arena without getting close to the source (Figure 6E, middle trace, 18%), while others headed downwind and remained at the downwind end of the arena (Figure 6E, right trace, 15%).
evidence: This is stated as a result from behavioral experiments.

claim: Model flies produced trajectories similar to those of real flies in the wind tunnel.
source: We observed that model flies produced trajectories similar to those of real flies in the wind tunnel.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: 66% of model flies successfully came within 2 cm of the odor source.
source: For example, some flies responded to odor with general movement upwind interrupted by occasional excursions out of the plume (Figure 6F); overall, 66% successfully came within 2 cm of the odor source.
evidence: This is stated as a result from model simulations.

claim: 17% of model flies searched but failed to locate the source.
source: Other model flies searched but failed to locate the source (17% of trials; Figure 6H, left trace), while others 'missed' the plume and moved downwind (17% of trials; Figure 6H, right trace).
evidence: This is stated as a result from model simulations.

claim: 17% of model flies 'missed' the plume and moved downwind.
source: Other model flies searched but failed to locate the source (17% of trials; Figure 6H, left trace), while others 'missed' the plume and moved downwind (17% of trials; Figure 6H, right trace).
evidence: This is stated as a result from model simulations.

claim: Using a single set of model parameters fit to the mean behavioral responses, the model yielded a similar although somewhat higher success rate than real flies (66% versus 56%).
source: Using a single set of model parameters fit to the mean behavioral responses in Figure 1F, we found that our model yielded a similar —although somewhat higher— success rate than real flies (Figure 6I, 66% versus 56% success rate).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Introducing variability in the model decreased the success rate to 45%.
source: Introducing variability in the model decreased the success rate to 45% (Figure 6I), and made it slightly worse than that of real flies in the wind tunnel.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The ON function was dominant throughout most of the odorized region in model trajectories.
source: We observed that the ON function was dominant throughout most of the odorized region, while excursions from the plume elicited strong OFF responses that frequently resulted in the model fly re-entering the plume.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Excursions from the plume elicited strong OFF responses that frequently resulted in the model fly re-entering the plume.
source: We observed that the ON function was dominant throughout most of the odorized region, while excursions from the plume elicited strong OFF responses that frequently resulted in the model fly re-entering the plume.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 6F-G.

claim: OFF responses were prominent near the odor source, contributing to the model fly lingering as observed in real flies.
source: OFF responses were also prominent near the odor source, where they contributed to the model fly lingering as observed in real flies.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 6F-G.

claim: ON and OFF magnitudes varied over a much smaller range than the range of odor concentrations.
source: ON and OFF magnitudes varied over a much smaller range than the range of odor concentrations, suggesting that the adaptive compression we incorporated into the model helps flies to respond behaviorally over a greater distance downwind of the source.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 6F-G and inferred from the model structure.

claim: Adaptive compression helps flies to respond behaviorally over a greater distance downwind of the source.
source: ON and OFF magnitudes varied over a much smaller range than the range of odor concentrations, suggesting that the adaptive compression we incorporated into the model helps flies to respond behaviorally over a greater distance downwind of the source.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of ON and OFF magnitudes in Figure 6F-G.

claim: ON responses are responsible for making flies progress within the odor area, allowing them to eventually reach the odor source.
source: This suggests that ON responses are responsible for making flies progress within the odor area, allowing them to eventually reach the odor source.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial distribution of ON shown in Figure 6J.

claim: The OFF function plays a role in relocating the plume after flies walk outside of it and the odor signal is lost.
source: The OFF function was most active in the area surrounding the odor plume (Figure 6K), suggesting it plays a role in relocating the plume after flies walk outside of it and the odor signal is lost.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial distribution of OFF shown in Figure 6K.

claim: The slow integration time of the OFF response may help it to detect the edges of the time-averaged plume.
source: This suggests that the slow integration time of the OFF response may help it to detect the edges of the time-averaged plume, allowing flies to slow down and search only when the plume has genuinely been exited.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that OFF values were generally low within the plume despite large fluctuations.

claim: Performance increased with both ON and OFF functions, but ON was more critical for success in the plume.
source: We observed that performance increased with both functions, but that ON was more critical for success in the plume, producing large improvements in performance as it increased.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6L.

claim: In a windless Gaussian gradient environment, success rates were lower and the contributions of ON and OFF were more similar.
source: In this environment, success rates were lower, but the contributions of ON and OFF were more similar, with higher success rates when the OFF function was the strongest for any given strength of the ON function.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6M.

claim: ON and OFF responses have different impact on success depending on the features of the environment.
source: These results suggest that ON and OFF responses have different impact on success depending on the features of the environment.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing results in Figure 6L and 6M.

claim: Walking Drosophila perform spatial comparisons across their antennae and turn toward the antenna that receives a higher odor concentration.
source: In addition to the ON and OFF functions described here, walking Drosophila have also been shown to perform spatial comparisons across their antennae, and to turn toward the antenna that receives a higher odor concentration (Borst and Heisenberg, 1982; Gaudry et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borst and Heisenberg, 1982 and Gaudry et al., 2013.

claim: Turns toward the antenna with higher odor concentration can be produced using optogenetic activation of olfactory receptor neurons in one antenna.
source: Such turns can be produced using optogenetic activation of olfactory receptor neurons in one antenna, arguing that they are independent of wind sensing (Gaudry et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gaudry et al., 2013.

claim: With a gain of 40 deg/s, spatial comparisons did not contribute significantly to the probability of successfully finding the source.
source: Based on the results of (Borst and Heisenberg, 1982) and (Gaudry et al., 2013), we estimated a gain of approximately 40 deg/s when the concentration difference between the two antennae is maximal. In this case, spatial comparisons did not contribute significantly to the probability of successfully finding the source (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: With a gain of 300 deg/s, performance of the model improved significantly from 67% to 76%.
source: However, if we increased the gain to 300 deg/s, we found that performance of the model improved significantly, from 67% to 76%.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: When the position of the antennae in the model was swapped, model flies were more prone to leave the area of the plume and wander off, decreasing their success rate to 54%.
source: We observed a contrary phenomenon when we switched the position of the antennae in the model, so that information from the right side was interpreted as left, and vice-versa. This made model flies more prone to leave the area of the plume and wander off, decreasing their success rate to 54% (Figure 7A–C, fourth column).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: In the absence of wind sensation, flies performing a correct bilateral comparison were unable to locate the odor source.
source: In the absence of wind sensation, flies performing a correct bilateral comparison were unable to locate the odor source (Figure 7A–C, fifth column).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Nearby locations in the plume contain information that can be used to aid navigation if the gain is high enough.
source: These results argue that nearby locations in the plume contain information that can be used to aid navigation (if the gain is high enough), but that this information is insufficient to find the odor source in the absence of wind.
evidence: This is concluded from the bilateral sensing simulations in Figure 7.

claim: Spatial information from bilateral comparisons is insufficient to find the odor source in the absence of wind.
source: These results argue that nearby locations in the plume contain information that can be used to aid navigation (if the gain is high enough), but that this information is insufficient to find the odor source in the absence of wind.
evidence: This is concluded from the bilateral sensing simulations in Figure 7.

claim: Some wind sensing is absolutely required to find the odor source, as almost no flies find the source when the wind coefficients are set to zero.
source: This analysis showed that some wind sensing is absolutely required to find the odor source, as almost no flies find the source when the wind coefficients are set to zero.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Both temporal sensing (OFF response) and spatial sensing (bilateral comparisons) contributed to increased performance in the plume.
source: In this case, we observed that both components contributed to increased performance.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Three different forms of sensing—flow sensing (wind), temporal sensing (OFF response), and spatial sensing (bilateral comparisons)—can all contribute to finding an odor source.
source: Together these results suggest that three different forms of sensation—flow sensing (wind), temporal sensing (OFF response), and spatial sensing (bilateral comparisons)—can all contribute to finding an odor source, but that the precise contribution of each mechanism depends both on the environment and on the gain or sensitivity of the animal to each measurement.
evidence: This is concluded from the simulations in Figure 7.

claim: The precise contribution of each sensing mechanism depends both on the environment and on the gain or sensitivity of the animal to each measurement.
source: Together these results suggest that three different forms of sensation—flow sensing (wind), temporal sensing (OFF response), and spatial sensing (bilateral comparisons)—can all contribute to finding an odor source, but that the precise contribution of each mechanism depends both on the environment and on the gain or sensitivity of the animal to each measurement.
evidence: This is concluded from the simulations in Figure 7.

claim: Olfactory navigation in complex environments can be decomposed into several largely independent sensori-motor transformations.
source: These data support the idea that olfactory navigation in complex environments can be decomposed into several largely independent sensori-motor transformations and provide a foundation for investigating the neural basis of these components.
evidence: This is concluded from the overall results of the study.
